summary: ob works with OpenBindings interface documents (OBIs): read and check them,

children.summary: Create a new document
children.description:
Create an OBI that declares OpenBindings 0.2.0 and has an empty
operations map, and write it to <obi>, laid out as ob fmt lays out a
document. Given - as <obi>, it writes the document to standard output. It
refuses to replace an existing file unless --force is given.

The options fill in the document's own fields. --interface-version sets
the interface-version label, the "version" field: the author's label for
the interface, which neither the specification nor ob interprets. It is
not the OpenBindings version the document declares, which is always
0.2.0. A label that is present must not be empty, so an empty
--interface-version is refused.

With --name "Task Manager" and --interface-version 1.0.0, ob init writes:

  {
    "openbindings": "0.2.0",
    "name": "Task Manager",
    "version": "1.0.0",
    "operations": {}
  }

From there, write operations in your editor and check the result with
ob validate (scripts use ob patch), or copy a shared contract's
operations in with ob merge. To start from an existing description such
as an OpenAPI document, add it as a source with ob source add and bring
its operations in with ob source pull.
children.examples:
# A document with a name and an interface-version label
  ob init tasks.obi.json --name "Task Manager" --interface-version 1.0.0

  # Print the new document instead of writing a file
  ob init - --name "Task Manager" \
    --description "Create, list and complete tasks."

  # Start from the operations of a shared contract
  ob init tasks.obi.json && ob merge tasks.obi.json acme-tasks.obi.json

  # Start from an existing OpenAPI description
  ob init tasks.obi.json --name "Task Manager" \
    && ob source add tasks.obi.json httpApi --kind example.openapi@1 \
         --data '{"fetch":"https://api.example.com/openapi.json"}' \
    && ob source pull tasks.obi.json httpApi

  # Start over, replacing an existing file
  ob init tasks.obi.json --name "Task Manager" --force
children.exitStatus:
0    the document was written
  2    bad arguments, such as a URL as <obi> or an empty
       --interface-version, or a file ob cannot write
  3    refused: the file exists and --force was not given; nothing was
       written
  See 'ob help exit-codes'.

children.summary: Show what a document describes
children.description:
Print an overview of a document: its name, interface-version label,
declared OpenBindings version and description; its operations, each with
its identifiers (key and aliases), its bindings and the dependencies that
consume it; then its sources, bindings, dependencies and named schemas.
To see one part in full, use the show command of its part: ob operation
show, ob binding show, ob dependency show, ob source show or ob schema
show.

<obi> is a path, - for standard input, or a URL. A bare origin such as
https://api.example.com is looked up at /.well-known/openbindings (HTTP
Discovery).

ob reads the declared version first. A text that declares a version
outside the 0.2 line is governed by that line, so ob never judges it by
0.2's rules: -F json prints its bytes, unchanged, and the overview
refuses it (exit 3), as other commands do (ob fetch still saves it).

Any other text is read under 0.2's rules, and ob show reads drafts: a
document that does not conform is still shown, with one warning naming
the rules involved and pointing to ob validate, and any part whose shape
is wrong is shown as unreadable, with its location; the exit status is
unaffected. Input that is not a JSON object meeting OBI-01 (UTF-8, with
no byte-order mark, repeated member name or unpaired-surrogate escape)
cannot be shown: ob prints its first findings and a hint to run
ob validate (exit 2). See 'ob help documents'.

-F json prints the document exactly as stored, rather than a report.
children.examples:
# An overview of a local document
  ob show tasks.obi.json

  # The document a service publishes at /.well-known/openbindings
  ob show https://api.example.com

  # The stored document, for jq and other JSON tools
  ob show tasks.obi.json -F json | jq '.operations | keys'

  # An earlier revision, read from standard input
  git show HEAD~1:tasks.obi.json | ob show -
children.exitStatus:
0    shown
  1    no OBI is published at the URL given
  2    bad arguments, a file that does not exist, input ob cannot read, or
       a network failure
  3    refused: the document declares a version outside the 0.2 line
       (without -F json)
  See 'ob help exit-codes'.

arguments.help: The document: a path, - for standard input, or a URL

children.summary: Check a document, values, or examples
children.description:
Check one of three things: each document against the rules of
OpenBindings 0.2, OBI-01 to OBI-14 (the default); with --operation and
--input or --output, values against that operation's input or output
contract; or, with --examples, each value an example gives against its
operation's value contract for that side. The document and examples
checks take several documents at once; --operation takes one.

Checking documents. The result for each document is one of:

  conformant                  every rule is met
  non-conformant              some rule is violated
  conformance undetermined    no rule is violated, but some rule could
                              not be decided

Each finding is one line on standard output:

  <document>:<line>:<column>: <rule>: <message> (at <pointer>)

<document> is the argument as given (<stdin> for standard input), so the
findings of several documents stay apart; line and column count from 1,
the column counts characters, and <pointer> is a JSON Pointer to the
place in the document. A last line for each document gives its result
and names the specification release and revision ob applied. A text that
is not JSON is non-conformant (OBI-01), not unreadable. A document that
declares another line, or a prerelease, is refused, not judged: see
'ob help documents'.

When an OBI-06 or OBI-08 finding is a binding or dependency that names
its operation by an alias, a hint follows it with the key that alias
identifies: "hint: acme.tasks.listTasks is an alias of listTasks;
bindings name operations by key".

When a document conforms, ob also checks its examples, and when any
example value fails its value contract it prints one warning pointing to
ob validate --examples, which lists each one. Examples are author claims,
which conformance does not judge (spec §5.1), so the warning never
changes the result or the exit status.

Checking values. --operation names the operation by key or alias. Each
--input is checked against its input contract and each --output against
its output contract, and one run may check both. A file or standard
input may hold several values separated by whitespace, each checked in
turn; only one argument may read standard input. Each result is labelled
by side and position (input 1, input 2, output 1) and is one of:

  satisfies      the value satisfies the value contract
  fails          the value fails the value contract; the problem is
                 given at a JSON Pointer into the value
  undefined      whether it satisfies the value contract is undefined (spec
                 §5.2), as when the answer rests on a pattern that is not
                 an ECMA-262 regular expression with Unicode semantics
  no-verdict     ob could not decide, and says why; for example, the
                 answer rests on an external schema, which ob names but
                 never fetches (ob schema bundle embeds it, so later
                 checks can decide)
  no-value-contract
                 the operation states no value contract for that side, so
                 the value neither satisfies nor fails one (spec §5.2)

Checking examples. --examples checks the examples of every operation of
each document, or with --operation, of that one. An example claims that
each value it gives satisfies the value contract for its side (spec
§5.1). A value given as null is a value, and is checked like any other.
Each value is reported in the words above, labelled by operation,
example and side. Where the operation states no value contract for a
side, the example makes no claim there: that value is listed as
no-value-contract and does not affect the exit status.

Values and examples need a conformant document: a non-conformant one is
refused (exit 3), and an undetermined one gets no verdict (exit 4). See
'ob help documents'.

For values and examples, one exit status covers each document: 1 if
anything fails; otherwise 4 if anything is undefined or no-verdict, or,
when checking values, no-value-contract (nothing was checked); otherwise
0.

Several documents. The document and examples checks take any number of
documents, at most one of them -, and check each in turn. --operation
takes one document (exit 2 otherwise), because values belong to one
operation. The exit status is the most serious across the documents: 2,
then 3, then 1, then 4, then 0, since a document that could not be read
or was refused leaves the run incomplete.

-q prints nothing and answers through the exit status alone. -F json
prints the report as JSON (see 'ob help output'): one report whose
documents array holds one entry per document, in the order given, even
for one, so a script reads the same shape however many documents a glob
matches. With --operation, it holds the one document's entry.
children.examples:
# Check a document against the rules
  ob validate tasks.obi.json

  # Check the document a service publishes, in a script
  ob validate https://api.example.com -q && echo conformant

  # In CI: check every document in a directory
  ob validate api/*.json -q

  # Check an input and a recorded output in one run
  ob validate tasks.obi.json --operation createTask \
    --input '{"title":"Plan the release"}' --output @response.json

  # Check every output value in a file; the alias identifies listTasks
  ob validate tasks.obi.json --operation acme.tasks.listTasks \
    --output @responses.json

  # Check the examples of every operation
  ob validate tasks.obi.json --examples
children.exitStatus:
0    every document conforms; or every value checked satisfies its
       value contract
  1    a document is non-conformant; or some value fails its value
       contract; or no OBI is published at a URL given
  2    bad arguments, such as --input without --operation or with
       --examples, --operation with nothing to check or with more than
       one document, or a value that is not JSON; a name or file that
       does not exist; a network failure
  3    refused: a document declares a version outside the 0.2 line; for
       values and examples, a document is non-conformant
  4    no verdict: a document's conformance is undetermined; or, for
       values and examples, nothing fails but a result is undefined or
       no-verdict; or, for values only, nothing fails but a side has no
       value contract to check
  With several documents, the most serious status wins: 2, then 3, then
  1, then 4, then 0.
  See 'ob help exit-codes'.

children.summary: Show what changed between two documents
children.description:
List the differences between two documents, part by part: the
document's own fields, then operations, sources, bindings, dependencies
and schemas. Each change names the part and its key, says whether it was
added, removed, changed or reordered, and gives a JSON Pointer to what
changed.

The documents are compared as JSON values, so layout, field order and
the spelling of a number (1.0 and 1) are not differences. ob fmt settles
layout and the order of the fields the specification defines; it keeps
number spelling (ob fmt --canonical writes one spelling, for hashing).
Array order is a difference, except in aliases, tags and kinds, whose
order means nothing to the specification: there a reorder, or for tags a
repetition (a repeated tag adds nothing), is reported as reordered, not
changed. --patch still turns <before> into <after> exactly.

ob diff reports differences only, not whether they matter to anyone who
calls the operations. To check whether <after> still serves the callers
of <before>, run ob compat <after> <before>, which treats <before> as the
shared contract.

--patch prints the differences as an RFC 6902 JSON Patch that turns
<before> into <after>; ob patch applies it to this or another document.
--exit-code makes the run a predicate: exit 1 when the documents differ,
0 when they do not. A change reported as reordered does not count, so a
CI gate does not fail over an order the specification gives no meaning.

-F json prints the differences as a report. Each change also carries the
exact values as stored: oldValue when it was removed, changed or
reordered, and newValue when it was added, changed or reordered; each is
absent when that side is absent.

Each argument is a path, -, or a URL; at most one may be -. Like ob show,
ob diff reads drafts, with one warning for each document that does not
conform: see 'ob help documents'.
children.examples:
# What changed between two versions
  ob diff tasks.obi.json tasks-next.obi.json

  # What changed since the last commit
  git show HEAD:tasks.obi.json | ob diff - tasks.obi.json

  # The change as a patch, to apply elsewhere with ob patch
  ob diff tasks.obi.json tasks-next.obi.json --patch > changes.json

  # In CI: fail when the published document differs from yours
  ob diff https://api.example.com tasks.obi.json --exit-code
children.exitStatus:
0    done; with --exit-code, the documents do not differ, other than
       in changes reported as reordered
  1    with --exit-code, the documents differ in a change that is not
       reordered; or no OBI is published at a URL given
  2    bad arguments, a file that does not exist, input ob cannot read, or
       a network failure
  3    refused: a document declares a version outside the 0.2 line
  See 'ob help exit-codes'.

children.summary: Check a document against a shared contract
children.description:
Check <obi> against a shared contract: for each operation of the shared
contract, which of <obi>'s operations its published names identify, and
whether their value contracts are compatible under the Schema Comparison
Profile OB-2020-12. With --dependency, check instead whether <obi> can
serve a dependency that <shared-contract> declares.

A shared contract is a published set of operations offered for adoption,
such as another OBI. Its operations' keys and aliases are published
names. An operation that carries a published name, as its key or as an
alias, claims correspondence with the operation that name identifies.

For each operation of the shared contract, ob compat reports:

  - which of <obi>'s operations its published names (its key and its
    aliases) identify, and whether by key or by alias; when they identify
    more than one, each is checked and listed;
  - whether the two operations' value contracts are compatible under the
    Schema Comparison Profile OB-2020-12, checked the way <obi> uses its
    operation:

    realized   it has bindings: it must accept every input the shared
               contract allows, and return only outputs it allows
    consumed   a dependency names it: it must send only inputs the
               shared contract accepts, and take every output it allows

An operation with both bindings and dependencies is checked both ways.
One with neither is checked as --check-as says: realized, consumed, or
both (the default). Where either operation states no value contract for a
side, that side is not compared. Operations of <obi> that carry no
published name of the shared contract are not part of the check.
--operation limits the check to the shared contract's operations it
names.

An operation of the shared contract that no operation of <obi> carries is
missing, and counts as incompatible. For each one, when <obi> is a path,
ob prints the two ways to claim it as hints: copy the shared contract's
operation in without its bindings, or give one of your operations its
published name as an alias.

  ob merge <obi> <shared-contract> --operation <name> --no-bindings
  ob merge <obi> <shared-contract> --operation <name> --onto <operation>

With -F json, the missing operation's entry carries the same two
commands as its remedies, each in two forms: command, the display
string, quoted for the shell, and argv, an array of its arguments, ob
first, in which each placeholder, such as <operation>, is its own
element, so a program can fill one in without re-quoting.

The result is compatible, incompatible, or indeterminate, combined as the
profile combines its outcomes: any indeterminate comparison makes the
result indeterminate; otherwise any incompatibility, a missing operation
included, makes it incompatible; otherwise it is compatible. The exit
status follows the result, so an indeterminate comparison beside a
definite incompatibility exits 4, not 1. In that case ob prints a
warning naming each operation found incompatible and each one missing,
and -F json lists each operation's verdict.

A keyword outside the profile, such as pattern or not, at a position
where the two schemas are not identical makes a comparison indeterminate
(identical positions are compatible, whatever keywords they use). What
the profile treats as an error rather than a verdict (a reference cycle,
an external schema, which ob never fetches, or an allOf no value can
satisfy) ob also reports as indeterminate, naming the cause.

For each incompatibility the profile gives a reason, prefixed by the
keyword that decided it and, for a nested failure, the path to it, such
as:

  required: candidate requires "extra" but target does not

With -F json, an issue's detail carries that reason verbatim, its prefix
and path included; the text output may say it in plain words.

Any OBI can serve as the shared contract. To check whether a new version
of a document breaks the callers of the old one, compare the new against
the old: ob compat new.obi.json old.obi.json. An operation renamed with
its old key kept as an alias still corresponds.

--dependency checks a candidate for a dependency. <shared-contract> is
then the document that declares the dependency, and <obi> is the
candidate, such as the OBI of a service that might serve it:

  ob compat <candidate> <document> --dependency <key>

ob reads the dependency <key> from <shared-contract>: the operation it
consumes, and its kinds. It checks that operation as --operation would,
but always as realized, since the candidate's bindings would carry the
calls. For each operation of <obi> that a published name (key or alias)
of the dependency's operation identifies, it lists that operation's
bindings, each with its source's kind, and marks each binding that meets
the dependency's kinds: its source's kind is the same string as one of
the kinds listed (spec §5.5, §6). A dependency without kinds accepts
every kind.

Each such operation is judged on its own. It serves when it has a
binding that meets the kinds and its comparison is compatible. It cannot
serve when no binding meets the kinds, whatever the comparison, or when
the comparison is incompatible. Otherwise, with a binding that meets the
kinds beside an indeterminate comparison, it gives no verdict. A
dependency needs one realization, so the answer is yes (exit 0) when
some operation serves; no verdict (exit 4) when none serves and some
gives no verdict; and no (exit 1) otherwise, including when the names
identify no operation. This is a different question from a whole shared
contract, whose summary follows the profile.

With -F json, the report adds dependency (its key, its operation, its
kinds when stated, and answer: serves, cannot-serve or no-verdict, which
decides the exit status), and each identified operation's entry adds
serving (the same three values) and its bindings (key, source, kind,
meetsKinds). The top-level verdict stays the profile's summary of the
comparisons made, which is not the dependency's answer: scripts read
dependency.answer. ob prints no merge hints here, and the report carries
no remedies: they would edit the candidate's document.

The check reads only the two documents. Whether this ob can invoke such
a binding is a question for ob kind list, and nothing records the
wiring: a dependency names no realization (spec §5.5). --dependency does
not combine with --operation or --check-as.

Both documents must conform: see 'ob help documents'. Each argument is a
path, -, or a URL; at most one may be -. -q prints nothing and answers
through the exit status alone.
children.examples:
# Which of Acme's task operations does tasks.obi.json correspond to?
  ob compat tasks.obi.json acme-tasks.obi.json

  # The same against a published shared contract, in a script
  ob compat tasks.obi.json https://acme.example.com/tasks.obi.json -q

  # Does the next version break callers of this one?
  ob compat tasks-next.obi.json tasks.obi.json

  # A new version of an unbound shared contract, checked as realized
  ob compat acme-tasks-v3.obi.json acme-tasks.obi.json --check-as realized

  # The service's published document, as a JSON report
  ob compat https://api.example.com acme-tasks.obi.json -F json

  # Can the notification service serve the assigneeNotifier dependency?
  ob compat https://notify.example.com tasks.obi.json \
    --dependency assigneeNotifier
children.exitStatus:
0    compatible; with --dependency, some operation of <obi> serves
       the dependency: it corresponds, is compatible, and has a binding
       that meets the dependency's kinds
  1    incompatible, a missing operation included; with --dependency,
       no operation serves and none gives no verdict; or no OBI is
       published at a URL given
  2    bad arguments, such as --dependency with --operation or
       --check-as; a name or file that does not exist, such as a
       dependency key <shared-contract> does not have; input ob cannot
       read; a network failure
  3    refused: a document is non-conformant or declares a version
       outside the 0.2 line
  4    indeterminate, even when an operation is also incompatible or
       missing, which a warning names; with --dependency, no operation
       serves and some gives no verdict; or a document's conformance is
       undetermined
  See 'ob help exit-codes'.

children.summary: Bring operations in from another document
children.description:
Copy operations from <from> into <obi> with the schemas, bindings and
sources they need: every named schema their value contracts reach
through references, transitively; their bindings; and the sources those
bindings go through. Dependencies are not copied: each is a consumption
point of <from>'s own described component. Each operation keeps its key
and aliases, so an operation copied from a shared contract carries its
published names, and so claims correspondence with the operation they
identify there. --operation limits the merge to the operations it names,
by key or alias in <from>. --no-bindings copies operations and their
schemas without bindings or sources.

ob never rebinds a copied reference silently, and never rewrites one. A
reference can reach into another operation of <from>, by JSON Pointer,
such as #/operations/listTasks/output, or through an $id declared there.
When the result keeps <obi>'s own version of that operation (it is not
being copied, it is skipped as already compatible, or --ours keeps it),
<obi> must hold an identical schema at that place, or under that $id.
Otherwise ob refuses (exit 3) and names the reference; when the operation
was not being copied, it hints --operation with that operation, which
then follows the conflict rules below.

Named schemas follow the same rule where <obi> already holds a key with
different content. --ours keeps <obi>'s schema, so a copied operation
that reaches it would reach a different contract than it does in
<from>: ob refuses (exit 3), names the reference, and hints ob schema
rename to make room. --theirs takes <from>'s schema, so it refuses
(exit 3) when operations outside the merge use the schema, and names
them: --operation limits the merge, and their contracts must not change
behind it. Its hint gives two ways on: ob schema rename one side's
schema first, or name those operations with --operation too, when
<from> has them. Identity decides, not compatibility: a compatible
schema is still a different contract.

Where <obi> already has an entry (the same key; for an operation, one
that the incoming operation's key or one of its aliases identifies):

  - an identical entry is left as it is;
  - an operation whose value contracts are already compatible with the
    incoming one's, checked as ob compat checks them (see --check-as
    below), is skipped as already compatible;
  - anything else, an indeterminate comparison included, is a conflict.
    ob lists every conflict and writes nothing, unless you choose a side:
    --ours keeps what <obi> has, --theirs takes what <from> has.

When an incoming operation's identifiers identify more than one
operation of <obi>, ob refuses (exit 3) and names them.

Where the match was by alias and the keys differ, --theirs keeps <obi>'s
key, so the bindings and dependencies that name it stay valid, and takes
<from>'s other fields. By key or by alias, the operation keeps its own
aliases and gains every identifier <from> gives it, its key and its
aliases, except the kept key, so each name that identified it in either
document still identifies it (spec §5.1). There is no option to replace
the aliases instead: like git's -X theirs, --theirs settles only what
conflicts, and dropping a name stays an edit of your own.

An operation <obi> already has, left as identical, or skipped as already
compatible when checked as realized, still brings the bindings <from>
has for it, and the sources they go through, unless --no-bindings: a
binding claims that its target realizes the operation as the document
describes it (spec §5.3), so the bindings of an operation compatible as
realized realize <obi>'s too. Binding and source keys that collide
follow the conflict rules above. Every binding merge brings in for an
operation matched by alias, copied with it under --theirs or brought in
this way, is written to name <obi>'s key, as ob operation rename
rewrites references.

--onto claims correspondence for an operation you already have, instead
of copying. It takes exactly one --operation, and adds the name given
there as an alias of the <obi> operation that --onto names, copying
nothing else. ob first compares the two operations' value contracts as ob
compat does. It refuses when the comparison establishes that they are
incompatible, and prints a hint with the ob patch command that adds the
alias directly, as your own claim (spec §5.1), which ob does not check;
there is no --force, so --onto always makes a checked claim. It goes
ahead with a warning when the comparison is indeterminate: carrying a
name is the author's claim, and only an established incompatibility
rules it out. It also refuses a name that already identifies another
operation of <obi>, since no name may identify two operations (OBI-05).

--check-as has ob compat's meaning (see 'ob help compat'), and applies
both to the skip check above and to --onto.

Both documents must conform, because merging relies on what they mean:
see 'ob help documents'. Like every edit, merge never writes a result
that violates a rule, warns about an example it makes fail, and changes
<obi> in place, or filters - to standard output (only one of <obi> and
<from> may be -); --dry-run prints the change instead of writing it.

A summary on standard error says what was added, what was skipped as
already compatible, which entries were replaced, and which aliases were
added. With -F json, the report adds them as four arrays: added (the
locations of the entries added, the bindings and sources brought for
operations <obi> already had included), skipped (the keys of the
operations skipped as already compatible), replaced (the locations of
the entries replaced) and aliasesAdded (the locations of the aliases
added to operations <obi> already had, by --onto or --theirs). When
there is nothing to bring in, the result is "no change".
children.examples:
# Copy in the operation that Acme's shared contract adds
  ob merge tasks.obi.json acme-tasks.obi.json \
    --operation acme.tasks.deleteTask --no-bindings

  # Or claim it for an operation you already have
  ob merge tasks.obi.json acme-tasks.obi.json \
    --operation acme.tasks.deleteTask --onto removeTask

  # Preview: add what is missing, keep your own where they conflict
  ob merge tasks.obi.json acme-tasks.obi.json --ours --dry-run

  # Operations you have not bound yet will be realized: check them so
  ob merge tasks.obi.json acme-tasks.obi.json --check-as realized \
    --dry-run

  # One operation from a newer version, without its bindings
  ob merge tasks.obi.json tasks-next.obi.json \
    --operation archiveTask --no-bindings

  # Start a new document from a shared contract
  ob init tasks.obi.json && ob merge tasks.obi.json acme-tasks.obi.json
children.exitStatus:
0    merged, or "no change"
  1    no OBI is published at the URL given as <from>
  2    bad arguments, such as a URL as <obi>, --ours with --theirs,
       --onto without exactly one --operation, or -F json without
       --dry-run when <obi> is -; a name or file that does not exist;
       input ob cannot read; a network failure
  3    refused: a conflict without --ours or --theirs; an incoming
       operation whose identifiers identify more than one operation of
       <obi>; a copied operation's reference that reaches into an
       operation, or a named schema, that the result keeps from <obi>,
       where <obi> holds no identical schema; --theirs replacing a named
       schema that operations outside the merge use; --onto with
       contracts established as incompatible (a hint gives the ob patch
       command that adds the alias), or with a name that already
       identifies another operation; a result that would violate a rule;
       a document that is non-conformant or whose conformance is
       undetermined; a version outside the 0.2 line
  See 'ob help exit-codes'.

children.summary: Apply a JSON Patch
children.description:
Apply an RFC 6902 JSON Patch to a document. The patch is read from the
file <patch>, or from standard input when <patch> is -. Its paths are
JSON Pointers into the document (RFC 6901), such as
/bindings/createTask.http/preference; a / inside a key is written ~1.

The patch applies whole or not at all. If any of its operations fails,
nothing is written. A test operation that does not hold is a definite no
(exit 1), so a patch can carry its own precondition; any other operation
that cannot apply, such as one whose path does not exist, exits 2.

ob patch applies the guard every edit applies (see 'ob help documents'):
it refuses a result that breaks a rule the document met, naming the
rule and where, with the findings in ob validate's format. A document
that already breaks rules can be repaired one patch at a time: a further
break of a rule it already breaks is written, with a warning for each
new finding. When it refuses a binding or dependency that names its
operation by an alias, the hint gives the key that alias identifies:
"hint: acme.tasks.listTasks is an alias of listTasks; bindings name
operations by key". Like every edit, it also warns about an example it
makes fail, and writes the change anyway.

ob patch is for scripts, and for changes no other command makes: setting
the interface-version label in a release pipeline, deprecating a
binding, adding an extension field. By hand, edit the document in your
editor, then run ob validate to check the result.

Like every edit, ob patch changes <obi> in place, keeping every byte the
patch does not touch, or filters - to standard output (with <patch> then
a file); --dry-run prints the change instead of writing it. With
-F json, the report holds the patch that would apply or was applied, and
adds no summary members. A patch whose result is already true is "no
change".
children.examples:
# Apply a patch file
  ob patch tasks.obi.json changes.json

  # Apply it, and read back the patch that was applied
  ob patch tasks.obi.json changes.json -F json | jq '.patch'

  # Set the interface-version label in a release pipeline
  echo '[{"op":"add","path":"/version","value":"1.5.0"}]' |
    ob patch tasks.obi.json -

  # See what a patch would change, without writing it
  ob patch tasks.obi.json deprecate-mcp.json --dry-run

  # Apply the change between two versions to another document
  ob diff tasks.obi.json tasks-next.obi.json --patch |
    ob patch tasks-staging.obi.json -

  # As a filter
  ob patch - changes.json < tasks.obi.json > tasks-next.obi.json
children.exitStatus:
0    applied, or "no change"
  1    a test operation in the patch does not hold; nothing was written
  2    bad arguments, such as a URL as <obi>, or -F json without
       --dry-run when <obi> is -; a file that does not exist; a patch or
       document ob cannot read; an operation that cannot apply
  3    refused: the result would violate a rule the document did not
       already violate, or the document declares a version outside the
       0.2 line
  See 'ob help exit-codes'.

children.summary: Format documents
children.description:
Rewrite each document with two-space indentation and ob's field order.
The root object, and each of its top-level maps that is not empty
(operations, sources, bindings, dependencies, schemas), always puts its
members one to a line, so the first member added never reflows the file.
Below them, an object or array is written on one line when that line is
at most 80 columns, and otherwise has its members one to a line.

The specification defines no layout; the layout is ob's own. The fields
of each object the specification defines come in the order its tables
list them: openbindings, name, version, description, operations,
sources, bindings, dependencies, schemas at the top; description,
deprecated, tags, aliases, input, output, examples in an operation;
kind, data, description in a source; operation, source, data,
idempotent, preference, description, deprecated in a binding; and so on
for dependencies and examples. Unknown fields, such as extensions,
follow in the order they had. Map entries (operations, sources,
bindings and the other maps) keep their order, and so do the members of
schemas, data and every other value.

Values are kept exactly: every number and string keeps its spelling, so
1.0 stays 1.0 and 1e3 stays 1e3. Formatting never changes a value.

--check changes nothing: it prints the name of each file that would
change and exits 1 if any would. --dry-run writes nothing and prints each
change as a unified diff. Together, --check --dry-run prints the diffs
and exits 1 if any file would change, as black --check --diff does. (fmt
takes no -F: formatting changes no value, so a JSON Patch of it would
always be empty.) Give - as <obi> to format standard input to standard
output; at most one <obi> may be -.

With several documents, ob formats each one it can, and the most serious
status wins: 2, then 3, then 1, then 0, since a document that could not
be read or was refused leaves the run incomplete.

--canonical prints the JSON Canonicalization Scheme form (RFC 8785) of
one document to standard output and writes nothing, for hashing and
signing (spec Appendix A), so it excludes --check and --dry-run
(exit 2). JCS sorts members, removes whitespace, and writes each number
from its binary64 value, so 1.0 becomes 1, the same number. ob refuses a
document that JCS cannot carry exactly (exit 3) rather than alter it:
one with a number whose value that rendering would change, such as
1000000000000000128, or other input RFC 8785 does not accept, such as a
number too large for binary64 or a noncharacter in a string.
children.examples:
# Format a document in place
  ob fmt tasks.obi.json

  # In CI: list documents that need formatting, and fail if any do
  ob fmt --check tasks.obi.json acme-tasks.obi.json

  # See what formatting would change
  ob fmt tasks.obi.json --dry-run

  # A stable digest of the document's value
  ob fmt --canonical tasks.obi.json | shasum -a 256

  # As a filter
  ob fmt - < tasks.obi.json > formatted.obi.json
children.exitStatus:
0    formatted, or already formatted; with --check, no file would
       change
  1    with --check, some file would change
  2    bad arguments, such as a URL, or --canonical with more than one
       document or with --check or --dry-run; a file that does not
       exist; input that is not JSON
  3    refused: --canonical on a document JCS cannot carry exactly, or a
       document that declares a version outside the 0.2 line
  With several documents, the most serious status wins: 2, then 3, then
  1, then 0.
  See 'ob help exit-codes'.

children.summary: Read, rename, and remove operations
children.description:
An operation is a named, protocol-independent capability contract under a
key in operations: what a service can do, with an optional input contract
and output contract that govern each value crossing its boundary (§3,
§5.1). Its key and its aliases are its identifiers, and a name identifies
the operation when it equals one of them (§5.1). Bindings declare
realizations of an operation (§5.3), and dependencies name points where
the described component consumes one (§5.5).

Commands here read operations, and rename or remove one while accounting
for every reference to it. You add an operation or change its fields
(description, aliases, tags, deprecation, input, output, examples) in your
editor, then run ob validate to check the result; scripts use ob patch,
which refuses a change that breaks a rule the document met.

children.summary: List operations, and how each is realized and consumed
children.description:
List each operation in document order: its key, its aliases, whether it
states an input contract and an output contract, the bindings that declare
realizations of it, the dependencies that consume it, and whether it is
deprecated.

An operation with bindings is realized, and one a dependency names is
consumed. An operation can be both, or neither.

With -F json, the report's operations array lists the same facts in
document order. A member copied from the document keeps its presence:
an operation with no aliases has no aliases member, and deprecated
appears only when the operation states it. bindings and dependencies
are always present, possibly empty.

In a document that does not conform, ob warns once and lists an operation
whose shape is wrong as unreadable, with its location (see
'ob help documents'). In JSON, such an entry is

  {"key": "<key>", "unreadable": true, "location": {...}}

and when the document's operations member is not an object, the
report's operations member, instead of an array, is

  {"unreadable": true, "location": {...}}
children.examples:
ob operation list tasks.obi.json
  ob operation list acme-tasks.obi.json
  ob operation list https://api.example.com -F json
children.exitStatus:
0    listed
  1    no OBI is published at the URL given
  2    the arguments are wrong, or <obi> cannot be read or fetched
  3    refused: the document declares a version outside the 0.2 line
  See 'ob help exit-codes'.

children.summary: Show one operation, named by its key or an alias
children.description:
Show the operation that <name> identifies, by its key or any of its
aliases (§5.1): its description, identifiers, input and output
contracts, examples, bindings and dependencies. --example shows one of
its examples alone.

The text shows:

  - its key, description and tags, and whether it is deprecated;
  - its aliases, the other names that identify it, such as the published
    names it carries. Carrying a shared contract's published name claims
    correspondence with that contract's operation (§5.1); ob compat
    checks such claims;
  - its input contract and output contract: the schema that states each,
    with references shown as written, or that none is stated;
  - its examples, each with the input and output values it gives, which
    ob validate --examples checks;
  - its bindings, each with its source and kind;
  - the dependencies that consume it, each with its kinds constraint.

--example <key> shows only the example under <key> in the operation's
examples, with the input and output values it gives. A key the
operation has no example under is a usage error (exit 2), with a
suggestion when one is close.

-F json prints the operation as stored, every value spelled exactly, and
nothing else; with --example, it prints that example as stored. The
operation's bindings and dependencies are stored elsewhere in the
document, so they are not included; ob binding list --operation lists
its bindings.
children.examples:
ob operation show tasks.obi.json createTask
  ob operation show tasks.obi.json acme.tasks.listTasks
  ob operation show tasks.obi.json notifications.send -F json
  ob operation show tasks.obi.json createTask --example basic -F json
children.exitStatus:
0    shown
  1    no OBI is published at the URL given
  2    the arguments are wrong, <obi> cannot be read or fetched, <name>
       identifies no operation, or the operation has no example under
       the --example key
  3    refused: <name> identifies two operations (OBI-05), the document
       declares a version outside the 0.2 line
  See 'ob help exit-codes'.

children.summary: Change an operation's key and every reference to it
children.description:
Change the key of the operation <name> to <new-name>, and update every
reference to it in the document: the operation field of each binding
and dependency that names it, and each same-document reference in the
document resource that points into the operation, however it is
spelled, such as {"$ref": "#/operations/createTask/input"} (§7.3).
--keep-alias also keeps the old key as an alias, so it still identifies
the operation.

Its other fields stay as they are, and so do its aliases unless
--keep-alias adds one: a plain rename only renames. ob changes only the
references the spec defines: data, descriptions and extension fields
are left alone, as is anything outside the document that uses the old
name, such as a script that runs ob invoke with it.

The old name then stops identifying the operation. If it was a shared
contract's published name, the operation no longer claims correspondence
through it. --keep-alias prevents that: it adds the old key to the
operation's aliases, creating the array when there is none, in the same
atomic write as the rename. This never breaks a rule the document met:
the old key was already unique and well-formed.

To keep the old name afterwards, or by hand, add it as an alias in your
editor or with ob patch. One RFC 6902 patch cannot both append to an
aliases array and create one, so the patch takes one of two shapes
(<old> is the old key, <new> the new one):

  when the operation has aliases:
    [{"op":"add","path":"/operations/<new>/aliases/-","value":"<old>"}]
  when it has none:
    [{"op":"add","path":"/operations/<new>/aliases","value":["<old>"]}]

<name> must be the key: given an alias, rename refuses and names the
operation whose alias it is. It refuses a <new-name> that already
identifies an operation, one of this operation's aliases included
(OBI-05), or that does not match the name grammar (OBI-04).

Like every edit, it changes <obi> in place, or filters - to standard
output, keeps the bytes it does not change, refuses a result that breaks
a rule the document met, and warns about an example it makes fail (see
'ob help documents'). --dry-run prints the change instead of writing
it. The summary on standard error names the alias --keep-alias added.
With -F json, the report adds the arrays renamed (the old key and the
new), updated (the locations of the references it updated) and, with
--keep-alias, aliasesAdded (the location of the alias added).
children.examples:
ob operation rename tasks.obi.json createTask addTask --keep-alias
  ob operation rename tasks.obi.json createTask addTask
  ob operation rename tasks.obi.json completeTask finishTask --dry-run
  ob operation rename tasks.obi.json listTasks findTasks --dry-run -F json
  ob operation rename - listTasks findTasks < tasks.obi.json > next.obi.json
children.exitStatus:
0    renamed, or no change (<new-name> is already its key)
  2    the arguments are wrong, such as -F json without --dry-run when
       <obi> is -; <obi> is a URL or cannot be read; or <name>
       identifies no operation
  3    refused: <name> is an alias or identifies two operations,
       <new-name> is taken or breaks the name grammar, the result would
       break another rule, or the document declares a version outside the
       0.2 line; nothing was written
  See 'ob help exit-codes'.

children.summary: Remove an operation
children.description:
Remove the operation <name>, with its aliases and examples. Its names
stop identifying anything, and any correspondence it claimed through them
goes with it.

It refuses while bindings or dependencies name the operation, and lists
them; --cascade removes those bindings and dependencies too. Sources and
named schemas stay, even when nothing uses them any more.

It also refuses while a reference from outside the operation reaches
into it, and lists each one with its location: a same-document reference
that points into it, such as {"$ref": "#/operations/createTask/input"} in
another operation's input, or a reference to an $id declared at or inside
its input or output. --cascade does not remove these: change them first,
in your editor or with ob patch.

<name> must be the key: given an alias, remove refuses and names the
operation whose alias it is. To drop only an alias, edit the operation's
aliases.

Like every edit, it changes <obi> in place, or filters - to standard
output, keeps the bytes it does not change, refuses a result that breaks
a rule the document met, and warns about an example it makes fail (see
'ob help documents'). --dry-run prints the change instead of writing
it. With -F json, the report adds the array removed (the operation's
key) and, with --cascade, the array cascaded (the locations of the
bindings and dependencies removed with it).
children.examples:
ob operation remove tasks.obi.json notifications.send --cascade
  ob operation remove tasks.obi.json completeTask --cascade --dry-run
  ob operation remove - createTask --cascade < tasks.obi.json
children.exitStatus:
0    removed
  2    the arguments are wrong, such as -F json without --dry-run when
       <obi> is -; <obi> is a URL or cannot be read; or <name>
       identifies no operation
  3    refused: <name> is an alias or identifies two operations, bindings
       or dependencies name it and --cascade was not given, a reference
       points into it or to an $id declared in it, the result would break
       another rule, or the document declares a version outside the 0.2
       line; nothing was written
  See 'ob help exit-codes'.

children.summary: Read bindings, and add one by hand
children.description:
A binding declares a realization of an operation through a source, under a
key in bindings (§3, §5.3). It names the operation and the source by their
keys (OBI-06, OBI-07). Where a binding names its operation by an alias,
ob validate gives a hint with the key, and in a document that meets
OBI-06, an edit that makes that change is refused with the same hint. Its
data is read under the source's kind, which decides what the data holds,
such as which target realizes the operation and how values are adapted
between the operation's contracts and that target (§5.3, §6). Its
idempotent field is an author claim, and its preference and deprecated
fields are author signals (§5.3).

ob source pull writes most bindings, with their operations. ob binding
add writes one by hand, in the form the source's kind describes, for an
operation you already have. You change, rename and remove bindings in
your editor, then run ob validate to check the result; scripts use
ob patch, which refuses a change that breaks a rule the document met.

children.summary: List bindings, with their operation, source and kind
children.description:
List each binding in document order: its key, the operation it binds,
the source it names, that source's kind, and the author's claim and
signals about it: its idempotent claim, its preference, and whether it is
deprecated. A binding whose source is not in the document shows no kind.

The idempotent claim is shown as stated: true, false, or absent, which
claims neither (§5.3). Preference and deprecation are author signals: a
higher preference states a stronger author preference among one
operation's bindings, and deprecated recommends migrating away (§5.3).
ob invoke shows them but does not choose a binding by them.

--operation lists only the bindings of the operation a name identifies,
given as its key or any alias.

With -F json, the report's bindings array lists the same facts in
document order. A member copied from the document keeps its presence:
idempotent, preference and deprecated appear only when the binding
states them, so an absent idempotent still claims neither. kind is
omitted when the binding's source is not in the document.

In a document that does not conform, ob warns once and lists a binding
whose shape is wrong as unreadable, with its location (see
'ob help documents'). In JSON, such an entry is

  {"key": "<key>", "unreadable": true, "location": {...}}

and when the document's bindings member is not an object, the
report's bindings member, instead of an array, is

  {"unreadable": true, "location": {...}}
children.examples:
ob binding list tasks.obi.json
  ob binding list tasks.obi.json --operation createTask
  ob binding list tasks.obi.json --operation acme.tasks.listTasks -F json
children.exitStatus:
0    listed
  1    no OBI is published at the URL given
  2    the arguments are wrong, <obi> cannot be read or fetched, or the
       --operation name identifies no operation
  3    refused: the --operation name identifies two operations (OBI-05),
       or the document declares a version outside the 0.2 line
  See 'ob help exit-codes'.

children.summary: Add a binding, as its source's kind describes it
children.description:
Add a binding under <key> that realizes the operation --operation names
through the source --source names, with data in the form the source's
kind describes. ob asks the Kind Descriptor for the kind's binding-data
schema (what ob kind describe shows) and fills it: from --data, or at a
terminal from what you enter for the schema's members. The data is what the
kind reads to carry out the operation: which target, and any adaptation
between the operation's contracts and that target, as the kind defines.
ob records it as given; the claim that the target realizes the operation
is yours, as for any binding (§5.3).

This is how a source realizes an operation you already have, including
one that ob source pull left out as a conflict because the source offers
it in a different shape; the hint pull printed gives this command. For
what a source offers under new keys, ob source pull adds operations and
bindings together.

--operation names the operation by its key or an alias; the binding is
written with the key, as bindings name operations (OBI-06). --idempotent
claims that repeating a call through this binding adds no further
intended effects; --idempotent=false claims it can; leaving it out claims
nothing. --preference records the author's preference among the
operation's bindings, which ob invoke shows and never chooses by.
--deprecated recommends migrating away.

Add needs this ob to support the source's kind for check, built in or
through a delegate, to show the schema and check the data. Without that
support, --data is recorded unchecked, with a warning; or write the
binding in your editor and run ob validate.

Like every edit, it changes <obi> in place, or filters - to standard
output, keeps the bytes it does not change, refuses a result that breaks
a rule the document met, and warns about an example it makes fail (see
'ob help documents'). --dry-run prints the change instead of writing it.
With -F json, the report adds the array added (the binding's key).
children.examples:
# At a terminal: answer the kind's binding schema
  ob binding add tasks.obi.json createTask.mcp --operation createTask \
      --source mcpServer

  # In a script: the data, as the kind's schema describes it
  ob binding add tasks.obi.json createTask.mcp --operation createTask \
      --source mcpServer --data '{"tool":"create_task"}'

  # By alias; the binding is written with the key, listTasks
  ob binding add tasks.obi.json listTasks.http \
      --operation acme.tasks.listTasks --source httpApi \
      --data '{"target":"#/paths/~1tasks/get"}' --idempotent

0    added, or an identical binding was already under <key>
  2    the arguments are wrong, such as -F json without --dry-run when
       <obi> is -, no --data without a terminal, or data the kind's
       schema does not accept; <obi> is a URL or cannot be read;
       --operation identifies no operation; or --source names no source
  3    refused: --operation identifies two operations (OBI-05), <key>
       already names a different binding, the result would break a rule,
       or the document declares a version outside the 0.2 line; nothing
       was written
  See 'ob help exit-codes'.

children.summary: Read dependencies
children.description:
A dependency is a named point where the described component consumes a
realization of an operation, under a key in dependencies; the key
identifies the consumption point (§3, §5.5). It names the operation by its
key (OBI-08), and may limit the kinds acceptable there with kinds, an
any-of constraint. It names no realization to serve it, not even one of
the document's own bindings (§5.5). Where a dependency names its
operation by an alias, ob validate gives a hint with the key, and in a
document that meets OBI-08, an edit that makes that change is refused
with the same hint.

To check a candidate for a dependency, such as the OBI of a service whose
bindings might serve it, run:

  ob compat <candidate> <obi> --dependency <key>

It judges each operation of the candidate that a published name (key or
alias) of the dependency's operation identifies: whether it is
compatible as realized, and which of its bindings, the realizations it
declares, have a source whose kind meets the dependency's kinds. Whether
this ob can invoke one is a question for ob kind list. ob dependency
show prints the command for its dependency.

Commands here read dependencies. You add, change, rename and remove
dependencies in your editor, then run ob validate to check the result;
scripts use ob patch, which refuses a change that breaks a rule the
document met.

children.summary: List dependencies, with their operation and kinds constraint
children.description:
List each dependency in document order: its key, which identifies the
consumption point, the operation it consumes, and its kinds constraint.

The kinds constraint is an any-of constraint: a binding meets it when its
source's kind is the same as one of those listed (§5.5). A dependency
without kinds places no constraint on kind, and is shown as accepting
every kind.

With -F json, the report's dependencies array lists the same facts in
document order. A member copied from the document keeps its presence:
kinds appears only when the dependency states it.

In a document that does not conform, ob warns once and lists a dependency
whose shape is wrong as unreadable, with its location (see
'ob help documents'). In JSON, such an entry is

  {"key": "<key>", "unreadable": true, "location": {...}}

and when the document's dependencies member is not an object, the
report's dependencies member, instead of an array, is

  {"unreadable": true, "location": {...}}
children.examples:
ob dependency list tasks.obi.json
  ob dependency list tasks.obi.json -F json

  1    no OBI is published at the URL given
  2    the arguments are wrong, or <obi> cannot be read or fetched
  3    refused: the document declares a version outside the 0.2 line
  See 'ob help exit-codes'.

children.summary: Show one dependency
children.description:
Show the dependency under <key>, the consumption point that key
identifies: the operation it consumes, its kinds constraint, and its
description.

Declaring a dependency claims that the described component sends only
input values that satisfy the operation's input contract, and takes any
output value that satisfies its output contract (§5.5); ob operation show
shows those contracts. The kinds constraint is an any-of constraint: a
binding meets it when its source's kind is one of those listed. Without
kinds, the dependency places no constraint on kind. A dependency names no
realization to serve it, so none is shown.

Then ob prints a hint with the command that checks a candidate for the
dependency, such as the OBI of a service that might serve it, leaving
<candidate> for you to fill in. For assigneeNotifier in tasks.obi.json:

  hint: ob compat <candidate> tasks.obi.json --dependency assigneeNotifier

See 'ob help compat' for the check.

-F json prints the dependency as stored, every value spelled exactly, and
nothing else.

ob dependency show tasks.obi.json assigneeNotifier
  ob dependency show tasks.obi.json assigneeNotifier -F json

children.summary: Read, rename, remove, and bundle schemas
children.description:
The schemas map holds named JSON Schemas, which operations and other
schemas reference, as in {"$ref": "#/schemas/Task"} (§5.2). Every schema
the document contains is read as JSON Schema 2020-12, and its references
resolve as §7 defines. An external schema is one a reference in the
document identifies, once resolved (against the enclosing $id, inside a
schema that declares one), that the document does not contain.

Commands here read schemas, rename or remove one while accounting for
every reference to it, and bundle external schemas into the document. You
add a schema or change one in your editor, then run ob validate to check
the result; scripts use ob patch, which refuses a change that breaks a
rule the document met.

children.summary: List named schemas, what references each, and external schemas
children.description:
List each named schema in document order, with its $id when it declares
one, and every reference to it: each $ref or $dynamicRef that identifies
the schema or a schema inside it, by JSON Pointer, plain name or $id,
shown with the reference's location.

Then it lists the external schemas: the resources that references identify,
once resolved against any enclosing $id and taken without their fragment,
that no schema the document contains declares as its $id. Each is shown with
the references to it. Resolving one needs that schema from outside the
document (§7.4). No check fetches it; ob schema bundle embeds it.

With -F json, the report holds a schemas array in document order and an
external array. A member copied from the document keeps its presence:
id appears only when the schema declares $id. references and external
are always present, possibly empty.

In a document that does not conform, ob warns once and lists a schema
whose shape is wrong as unreadable, with its location (see
'ob help documents'). In JSON, such an entry is

  {"key": "<key>", "unreadable": true, "location": {...}}

and when the document's schemas member is not an object, the
report's schemas member, instead of an array, is

  {"unreadable": true, "location": {...}}

children.summary: Rename a named schema and every same-document reference to it
children.description:
Change the key of the schema <key> in schemas to <new-key>, and update
every same-document reference to it in the document resource: each $ref
and $dynamicRef whose JSON Pointer reaches the schema or a schema inside
it, such as #/schemas/Task or #/schemas/Task/properties/id. That includes
spellings that identify it once percent-decoded, such as
#%2Fschemas%2FTask (§7.3). An updated reference keeps its spelling except
for the name.

against that schema's own base, not against the document (§7.2, §7.4).
References through the schema's $id, or through a plain name it declares,
do not contain its key and keep working. Other documents reach a schema
only through an $id, which the rename does not change (§7.5). Content,
examples, descriptions and extension fields are left alone.

It refuses a <new-key> that another schema already has, or one that does
not match the name grammar (OBI-04).

Like every edit, it changes <obi> in place, or filters - to standard
output, keeps the bytes it does not change, refuses a result that breaks
a rule the document met, and warns about an example it makes fail (see
'ob help documents'). --dry-run prints the change instead of writing
it. With -F json, the report adds two arrays: renamed (the old key and
the new) and updated (the locations of the references it updated).

children.summary: Embed the external schemas the document references
children.description:
Fetch each external schema the document references (resolved against any
enclosing $id), by its URI without the fragment, and embed it under schemas
with that URI as its $id. References do not change: references to the URI
now resolve to the embedded copy, as JSON Schema's bundling defines (§7.2,
§7.4), so the document no longer needs that schema from outside. External
schemas that a copy references in turn are bundled too. Given <uri>
arguments, it bundles only those, and what they reference in turn.

This is the one command that fetches external schemas, and it embeds
what it fetches. Checks never fetch one, so bundling is what lets them
decide, and lets ob invoke call an operation whose value contracts
reference one.

ob fetches https and http URIs, sending no credentials of its own.

It refuses a fetched schema that declares an $id other than its URI, or a
$schema other than 2020-12 (OBI-09), and names the URI and the reason.
Nothing is written, so every schema stays external; name the other URIs
to bundle them without it. A URI that cannot be fetched stops the bundle
in the same way.

Each copy's key comes from its URI, such as date-time for
https://schemas.example.com/date-time.json, made unique among the
document's schemas. ob schema rename changes the key, and references keep
resolving through the $id.

Like every edit, it changes <obi> in place, or filters - to standard
output, keeps the bytes it does not change, refuses a result that breaks
a rule the document met, and warns about an example it makes fail (see
'ob help documents'). --dry-run still fetches, and prints the change
instead of writing it. With -F json, the report adds the array added
(the keys of the schemas embedded).

children.summary: Add sources and pull what they offer
children.description:
A source is what a document reads operations and bindings from, under a
key in sources: an exact kind, which names how the source's data and its
bindings' data are read (§5.2, §6), and that data, whatever the kind
defines for it: an embedded description such as an OpenAPI document, the
URL of one read on every use, the command line of a server, or nothing at
all. Bindings name a source and carry data of their own, read under the
same kind (§5.3).

add puts a source in a document the way its kind describes: ob shows the
kind's own schema for the data, fills it from your answers or --data, and
has the kind check and complete the entry before writing it. pull reads a
source under its kind and brings what it offers into the document: new
operations, the schemas they need and bindings naming the source, applied
directly, with proposals for what it would change and a report of what it
left out. list, show, rename and remove work with any kind, since they
read nothing under it.

What a source's data means, and what the kind consults to read it, is the
kind's definition. ob never interprets it: it shows the kind's schemas,
records what the kind returns, and keeps the data exactly as stored.
ob kind list shows which kinds this ob supports, and for which
operations: check (ob source add), pull (ob source pull) and invoke
(ob invoke), ob's names for the Kind Descriptor's checkSource, the Source
Puller's pullSource and the Binding Invoker's invokeBinding.

List each source in document order: its key, its kind, its description,
the number of bindings that name it, and which of check, pull and invoke
this ob supports for its kind, built in or through a delegate, as ob kind
list reports it. A source whose kind this ob supports for nothing is still
listed; a document may use any kind.

With -F json, the report's sources array lists the same facts in
document order: key, kind, description when stated, bindingCount, and
supports, the operations this ob supports for the kind, by their keys,
each with its provider (built-in, or a delegate's registration ID).

In a document that does not conform, ob warns once and lists a source
whose shape is wrong as unreadable, with its location (see
'ob help documents'). In JSON, such an entry is

  {"key": "<key>", "unreadable": true, "location": {...}}

and when the document's sources member is not an object, the report's
sources member, instead of an array, is

  {"unreadable": true, "location": {...}}

ob source list tasks.obi.json
  ob source list tasks.obi.json -F json
  ob source list https://api.example.com

0    listed
  1    no OBI is published at the URL given
  2    the arguments are wrong, or <obi> cannot be read or fetched
  3    refused: the document declares a version outside the 0.2 line

children.summary: Add a source, as its kind describes it
children.description:
Add a source under <key>, in the form its kind describes. ob asks the
Kind Descriptor for the kind's source-data schema (what ob kind describe
shows) and fills it: from --data, or at a terminal from what you enter
for the schema's titled branches and members. It then has the kind check the
entry (the Kind Descriptor's checkSource) and return the one the kind
stands behind, completed as the kind defines (a description fetched and
embedded, a server's name read, a default filled), and writes that. What
the data means is the kind's; ob records what the kind returns.

--kind names the kind; without it, at a terminal, ob lists the kinds it
supports for check and asks. --data gives the data as the schema
describes it: JSON, @FILE, or - for standard input. Without --data, at a
terminal, ob prompts from the schema; without a terminal, --data is
required. A kind's check may need context, such as a token to read a
description behind sign-in: ob asks at a terminal, offers to store the
answer for the source (ob context set), and otherwise stops (exit 3) and
prints the command that supplies it. Before a check that runs something,
such as starting a server to read it, ob says what the kind's check does
and asks; --yes answers for a script.

A source already under <key> is replaced only when you confirm at a
terminal or give --replace; an identical one is no change. Replacing a
source is how a document takes a newer description: ob reads nothing
behind an embedded document on its own, so bringing a new version in is
your act, and ob source pull then brings in what changed.

The document gains one source and no operations or bindings; ob source
pull adds those. Add needs this ob to support the kind for check, built
in or through a delegate; ob kind list --supports check shows which kinds
it does.

Like every edit, it changes <obi> in place, or filters - to standard
output, keeps the bytes it does not change, refuses a result that breaks
a rule the document met, and warns about an example it makes fail (see
'ob help documents'). --dry-run runs the check and prints the change
instead of writing it. With -F json, the report adds the array added
(the source's key), or replaced when a source was replaced.
children.examples:
# At a terminal: pick the kind, then answer its schema
  ob source add tasks.obi.json httpApi

  # In a script: the kind and its data, as the kind's schema describes it
  ob source add tasks.obi.json httpApi --kind example.openapi@1 \
      --data '{"fetch":"https://api.example.com/openapi.json"}'

  # A description you already have, embedded in the form the kind takes
  jq '{artifact: .}' openapi.json | ob source add tasks.obi.json httpApi \
      --kind example.openapi@1 --data -

  # Take a newer description, then pull what changed
  ob source add tasks.obi.json httpApi --kind example.openapi@1 \
      --data '{"fetch":"https://api.example.com/openapi.json"}' --replace
  ob source pull tasks.obi.json httpApi

  2    the arguments are wrong, such as -F json without --dry-run when

       schema does not accept; <obi> is a URL or cannot be read; or the
       kind's check failed, saying what is wrong
  3    refused: <key> names a different source and --replace was not
       given, this ob does not support the kind for check, the check
       needs context ob cannot ask for, a check that executes was not
       confirmed, the result would break a rule, or the document declares
       a version outside the 0.2 line; nothing was written
  See 'ob help exit-codes'.

children.summary: Pull what a source offers into the document
children.description:
Read each source named, under its kind, and bring what it offers into the
document: for each item the source offers, an operation, the schemas it
needs, and a binding naming the source. With no <key>, every source is
pulled, one at a time. Pull reads the source as the document holds it: an
embedded description from the document, a referenced one from where its
kind says, and nothing else; what a kind consults is its definition,
which ob kind describe shows.

What pull writes, and what it leaves to you:

  - Additions are applied: new operations, schemas and bindings, under
    keys new to the document, so nothing is overwritten. When the source
    offers an operation under a key the document already has, pull
    compares the offered input and output contracts with the existing
    ones: equal, it binds the source to the existing operation and says
    so (reused); different, it leaves the item out as a conflict and says
    why, and you bind it by hand with ob binding add, adapting in binding
    data as the kind defines, or add it under another key.
  - Changes are proposals: a binding the source still offers but would now
    write differently (stale), a schema it offers that the document holds
    differently, or, for a kind that may refresh its own source data, the
    source entry itself. A proposal carries only what the kind owns (a
    binding's data, an operation's input or output contract, a schema,
    the source's data), never your description, preference or idempotent
    claim, and the kind's judgment of the change: breaking, dangerous or
    non-breaking. --force applies every proposal; --force=<entry> applies
    the named one, and may repeat.
  - Removals are yours: a binding the source no longer offers (unmatched)
    is listed and left; --prune removes unmatched bindings. ob never
    removes an operation; the hint names ob operation remove when one has
    no bindings left.

The report names each item the source offers that pull did not represent
(omitted), with the reason: excluded by a rule of the kind, invalid in the
source, not supported by this ob's implementation of the kind, or a
conflict with an existing operation. It says whether the source was read
in full (exhaustive) and, if not, why. Pulling again changes nothing.

--check writes nothing: it runs the pull and exits 1 when anything is
stale or unmatched, so a CI job fails when a document falls behind its
sources; for a source embedded in the document, that is a document whose
bindings no longer match what it holds, and a job that wants to catch the
API itself drifting re-adds the source from its description first. --dry-run
shows what a pull would apply without writing it. --no-reuse leaves out
every item that would reuse an existing operation, as a conflict, instead
of binding to it.

A kind may need context to read a source, such as a token: ob uses what
ob context set stored for the source, asks at a terminal, and otherwise
stops (exit 3) and prints the ob context set command that supplies it.

Pull relies on what the document means, so it refuses a document that is
non-conformant or whose conformance is undetermined (exit 3), and never
writes a result that violates a rule. Like every edit, it changes <obi>
in place, or filters - to standard output (see 'ob help documents'). With
-F json, the report holds what ob wrote: the patch applied and, per
source, the Source Puller's report exactly as returned (added, existing,
omitted, exhaustive), so a script reads what was applied and what waits.
children.examples:
ob source pull tasks.obi.json
  ob source pull tasks.obi.json httpApi
  ob source pull tasks.obi.json httpApi --force
  ob source pull tasks.obi.json httpApi --force=completeTask.http \
      --force=Task
  ob source pull tasks.obi.json httpApi --prune
  ob source pull tasks.obi.json --check
  ob source pull tasks.obi.json httpApi --dry-run
  ob source pull tasks.obi.json -F json | jq '.sources[].report.existing'

  1    with --check: something is stale or unmatched
  2    the arguments are wrong, such as -F json without --dry-run when
       <obi> is -, --check with --force, --prune or --dry-run, --force
       beside --force=<entry>, or a --force=<entry> that names no

       rule, or the document declares a version outside the 0.2 line;
       nothing was written
  See 'ob help exit-codes'.

children.description:
Download the OBI a service publishes and print it to standard output,
byte for byte as served, or save it with -o. A bare origin such as
https://api.example.com is looked up at /.well-known/openbindings (HTTP
Discovery 0.1); any other URL is fetched as given. ob follows redirects.

ob sends no credentials of its own: a URL that answers 401 or 403 is one
ob cannot read (exit 2). Fetch such a document with a tool that can sign
in and give ob the result on standard input, as every command that takes
a document accepts it (curl -H 'Authorization: Bearer ...' URL | ob show -).

ob saves any response that declares an OpenBindings version (§8.1),
whatever the line: one that declares another line unchanged, with a
warning that this ob reads 0.2, and a 0.2-line document that does not
conform, or whose conformance is undetermined, with a warning naming the
rules and pointing to ob validate. A response that is not JSON, or
declares no version, is not saved.

Commands that read a document, such as ob show and ob invoke, also take a
URL and fetch it the same way; fetch is for keeping a copy.
